newsitem.title: USA: Sharp Dow slide, profit-taking weaken dollar in US.
newsitem.headline: Sharp Dow slide, profit-taking weaken dollar in US.

text.p: Pressured by a sharp fall in stocks, the dollar succumbed to a heavy bout of pre-weekend profit-taking and ended broadly lower on Friday.
A sharp morning selloff followed a report from the Commerce Department which showed that the U.S. trade deficit flared to a wider-than-expected $10.23 billion in May from $8.75 billion in April.
But dealers said the losses were only indirectly related to the trade report and pointed to the greenback's failure to hold above the key 1.80 mark threshold for a fourth consecutive session.
"Today was a day to take some profits," said a senior dealer at a European bank in New York. "We probed the 1.80 mark level again and we just weren't able to hold above it."
The dollar ended at 1.7920/30 marks, down from its session high of 1.8005 and off its opening level of 1.7990/00.

After rising briefly above the 116 yen level on news that that the politically sensitive bilateral deficit with Japan shrank by 25 percent in May to $3.63 billion, the dollar closed at 115.55/65 yen, down from 115.75/85 at the open.
A sharp tumble in the Dow Industrials, which ended the day near its session lows, down 130 points at 7890, provided added incentive for traders looking to secure their profits ahead of the weekend.
Nonetheless, traders were confident that the dollar, supported by a strong U.S. economic backdrop, could resume its upward trajectory next week.
"The drop in the Dow did happen to impact sentiment and aid in selling the dollar off," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president of foreign exchange sales at Credit Agricole Indosuez.
"But the fundamentals are still working in the dollar's favor," he added.
Keeping the dollar's losses against the mark contained were further signs that German officials are not overly concerned with dollar/mark's strength.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Friday that the dollar's recent strength against the mark was not "earth shaking."
The comments followed similar remarks from Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp who said on Thursday that the dollar's recent rise was "nothing spectacular."
"The comments coming out of Germany seem to say they are not concerned," said the senior dealer. "I think this is what the Europeans have wanted for quite some time."
Traders said the dollar needed a near-term move above the 1.8050 mark level to fuel further gains. Conversely, they said a decline below 1.7850 marks would accelerate a move to the downside.
Late Friday the market was looking ahead to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony next Tuesday.
Next week's Bundesbank council meeting will also garner a great deal of attention, dealers said.
In other trade on Friday, the dollar ended at 1.4750/60 Swiss francs, down from 1.4828/38 at the open, and fell to Canadian $1.3744/49 from C$1.3759/64.
Sterling rose to $1.6785/95 from $1.6728/38, while the Australian dollar ended the week at $0.7415/20, up from $0.7394/99.
(( -- Noah Barkin, N.A. Forex Unit, 212-859-1673 ))
